title: What Einstein Really Thought About Religion
the_thought: He thought God was the order of the universe, not a person who listens.
hook: Einstein talked about God his whole life. Then people treated his religion like a vote. He thought God was the order of the universe, not a person who listens. Churches quoted him. Atheists quoted him. Yet they were reading two different men. Why?

levels.name: The Telegram
beats: April, 1929. A rabbi in New York pays for a cable. Five words. Do you believe in God. A cardinal in Boston has just said relativity cloaked the ghastly apparition of atheism. The rabbi wants a yes he can print. Einstein answers in German. Twenty-five words. He believes in Spinoza's God, who reveals himself in the lawful harmony of the world. Not in a God who concerns himself with the fate and the doings of mankind. Newspapers run it. Some readers hear a believer. Some hear a man saying no, politely. Which is it?

levels.name: The Door
beats: Here's what most versions skip. He was the son of irreligious parents. Then, as a boy, he became intensely devout. Bible. Talmud. The whole furniture of belief. Around twelve, science books arrived. He later wrote that this religiosity ended abruptly. Cause and effect would not share a room with miracle stories. He did not turn into a professional atheist. Years later he said he did not share that crusading spirit. He thought it was often a leftover from childhood. A slammed door that still makes a noise. He slammed the door too. He just refused to say the house was empty.

levels.name: The Nickname
beats: Because he would not stop saying God. In 1926 he writes to a physicist friend. Quantum theory is impressive, he says. It does not bring us closer to the secret of the Old One. He is convinced He is not playing at dice. People print it like a prayer. It is not a prayer. It is a fight about whether the universe is random. In that sentence, God is a nickname for the law. If the law rolls dice, the nickname fails. He tells an interviewer he is not an atheist. He says even the smartest person is like a child walking into a huge library. The books are in languages the child cannot read. Someone wrote them. The child feels an order and cannot name the author. That is humility. It is not a church, and it is not a sneer.

levels.name: The Letter
beats: Near the end of his life, a philosopher sends him a book that treats the Bible as a living call. Einstein sits in Princeton and answers in his own handwriting. The word God, he writes, is for him nothing but the expression and product of human weaknesses. The Bible, a collection of venerable but still primitive legends. No clever reading can change that for him. He adds that the Jewish religion, like the others, is an incarnation of primitive superstition. And in the same letter he says he gladly belongs to the Jewish people. Atheists frame the page. Believers call it a fake. It is neither a conversion nor a prank. It is the same split he cabled twenty-five years earlier. A listening God: no. A chosen people: no. Awe at the order: still yes.

levels.name: The Feeling
beats: He had a name for that awe. Cosmic religious feeling. No dogma. No God with a human face. In an essay he argued that people doing serious science were, in that sense, the deeply religious ones. Not because they prayed. Because they trusted the world to make sense, and they were moved by it. So what did he really think about religion? He thought God was the order of the universe, not a person who listens. He would not kneel, and he would not enlist in the war on kneeling. If you needed a father in the sky, he would fail you. If you needed a universe that was only junk, he would fail you too.
The word still causes trouble. Because the next fight is not God. It is what he thought when people used God to run a nation. That story is next.
